# The Cognitive Debt of the AI Generation

@christiansafka · Nov 22, 2026

Cognitive Debt, or “AI brain rot” is potentially the most dangerous side effect of rising global AI use, yet when we talk about AI safety research it is rarely included.

In this blog, I’ll try to summarize what has been measured so far in academic work, debate the future of work and intelligence, and suggest what we can individually do to mitigate cognitive decline.

## What is Cognitive Debt?

> Cognitive debt is the long-term cost to human understanding, critical thinking, or mental stamina that builds up when people shortcut mental effort—most notably by over-relying on AI tools.

In “ Your Brain on ChatGPT ” from MIT Media Lab , 54 participants wrote essays using ChatGPT, a search engine, or no tools while researchers measured brain activity with EEG. The un-aided group showed the strongest measured brain connectivity, the search group less, and the ChatGPT group the least. LLM users struggled to recall their essays and felt the least ownership over their writing.

What we learned from this is that brain connectivity is higher if you write on your own, but this doesn’t yet directly correlate with intelligence.

So why did brain activity decrease in the ChatGPT-user group, and should we consider it a cognitive decline?

> Neural efficiency in the field of neuroscience suggests that a beginner solving a math problem may activate a lot of connections, while an expert solving the same problem may use more sparse connections efficiently.

With AI, the task of writing became a simple task. The author could focus on the high-level ideas in the prompt, letting the LLM handle the details. This is analogous to what most software engineering has become in 2026.

Could it be that the ChatGPT-using author was using sparse brain connections more efficiently? Or was there simply less learning happening? This is the question many are asking themselves as they move from executor to supervisor, managing higher and higher level decisions and abstractions of their work. Let’s review more research:

A study of sixty young adults found that those who habitually relied on GPS had reduced spatial memory. Another 2025 study of 666 participants (this study, brought to you by Satan) found a significant negative correlation between frequent AI usage and critical thinking abilities.

If we passively accept AI assistance for more and more of our critical thinking, it would appear we’ll lose these skills. If this happens on a societal level, we would be fully dependent on AI to make the right decisions for us, with no ability to connect the dots ourselves to evaluate or fix its mistakes.

### Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)

> What if we achieve AGI that makes no mistakes? Or at least exceeds human capability on all tasks?

Now we can debate: Today we value intelligence because it helps us achieve things. If AGI achieves those things better, perhaps intelligence will no longer be valuable.

The theory is that humans can instead spend their time on sports, creative work, and social interactions.

However a comfortable life isn’t necessarily a fulfilling one. Humans are driven by a purpose, to achieve mastery of something, to overcome a struggle, to contribute to society, and to make ourselves proud of what we are capable of.

> But couldn’t we still choose to do hard things?

Sure, but if there’s no economic or cultural value in them, will there be motivation?

AGI arriving won’t be like flicking a switch to a dystopian world; it will happen gradually over a long period of societal adjustment. In 2026 we would expect the majority of people to believe AI should not replace critical thinking for us, for a variety of reasons. Over time this may change, particularly once there is little economic reason to put in effort.

Today, however, it is far too early for us to begin our cognitive decline, and those who don’t lose their mental acuity will still be rewarded.

### So what can we do today to preserve our minds?

As a technical founder, delegating to AI is table stakes for moving fast with a small team – and I wouldn’t suggest anyone simply ignore AI.

I’ve found that writing has been incredibly helpful for solidifying my thought process behind decisions, as well as helping uncover gaps in my understanding. The MIT study also backs this method. As a bonus, writing lets you bring your unique content, voice, and opinions to the world. While long-term effects of this remain understudied, being conscious of how much you’re offloading to AI, and intentionally practicing reflection and critical thinking, can be a powerful way to combat AI brain fog.
